subject: jukebox
pitch: A 1950s diner jukebox. A tall rounded arch of glowing coloured tubes in red, amber and teal, chrome trim everywhere, a domed glass window showing a stack of records and the arm that picks them, rows of chrome selection buttons with little title cards, a speaker grille with a starburst pattern, and a coin slot.

I'm sketching the three main sections: a wide base cabinet with chrome kick plate, starburst speaker grille and coin slot, a middle selection panel with chrome buttons and title cards, and a crowning glass-domed arch glowing with red, amber, and teal tube lights arranged to evoke the classic Wurlitzer "bubble" lighting effect.

Now I'm roughing out concrete measurements—overall height around 1.6m, width 0.75m, depth 0.6m—and planning to build the body from simple boxes rather than rounded geometry, keeping things blocky and puppet-like while staying within documented builder APIs like joint creation to avoid runtime errors.

I'm also noting other builder primitives like slab, decal, cards, rod, capsule, spike, and frustumBox, plus utility functions like paint and texture helpers (mottle, gradient, noise, etc.) and math helpers (rng, frame, lerp, catmull, bezier). Everything comes from the single SDK module, so I should import all needed exports from 'agentic-3js-builder' rather than per-file paths.

Now I'm thinking about whether scenery objects without a skeleton still need a root joint, since the system requires exactly one root joint and a second one throws an error -- I need to check if createBuilder auto-generates that root.

For a jukebox prop, I'm deciding whether to create a single root joint like "cabinet" at the origin, and whether to add a couple of functional joints too, like a pick-arm chain or a hinge for the glass dome lid, keeping the rig minimal since detailed rigging only really matters for creatures.

I'm also now budgeting the part count against the 1000-part limit, roughly sketching out how many buttons, title cards, and stacked records a stylized Wurlitzer-style jukebox would need.

Since triangle counts are well under the 60k cap, I'm instead focused on how to fake the classic glowing tube look without emissive materials or scene lights available in the SDK — settling on bright, saturated colors like red, amber, and teal to suggest luminosity through hue alone rather than actual glow effects.

For the tubes, I'm thinking of using sectors to add a lighter "hot" stripe along the facing side, mimicking a lit glass core. For the dome housing the record stack, true transparency isn't available in the SDK materials, so I'm considering a thin pale-colored lathe shell with an open front instead of a fully opaque dome that would hide the mechanism inside.

Since lathe and sweep geometries can't easily have holes cut into them, I'm thinking the simplest solution is building the dome from partial panels with gaps between them, letting the records inside show through the openings where the "glass" isn't present rather than trying to fake transparency.

My final decision: make the window a recessed chrome-framed opening with a birdcage-style dome of arc ribs — vertical ribs spanning left to right plus horizontal bands — so the gaps reveal a dark velvet backdrop and the record stack behind.

I'll depict the records as a vertical stack of flat discs with alternating label colors, stacked like coins, with a chrome arm reaching toward them, rather than records standing on edge in a carousel — keeping the pale-glass illusion coming from the ribs and tint rather than any actual transparency.

Now I'm sketching the full front-facing layout numerically: starting with a chrome kick plate at the base roughly 0.72 wide, 0.1 high, 0.55 deep, then building up the lower cabinet body above it.

Thinking through the lower body shape, I'm weighing whether to use a loft with elliptical versus rectangular cross-sections to get that classic rounded jukebox bulge, leaning toward treating it as a box-section sweep since that seems the safer, more predictable approach.

Actually, since the puppet's art direction wants that blocky, primitive-built look, I don't need true roundness — boxes and frustum boxes work fine for the body, with an extrude used to capture the side silhouette (tall body, arched top profile) by drawing the outline in the side plane and giving it thickness along the width axis.

Now I'm sketching the overall composition: the front view carries the main visual read (width, controls, arch of tubes), while the side profile adds the characteristic depth — deep cabinet base, narrower bulging head at top. I'm roughing out approximate dimensions in meters to block out the cabinet, head, and arch before building each piece.

I'm deciding to build each section using straightforward box geometries positioned with explicit coordinates rather than relying on an ambiguous frustum helper, since direct boxes are more predictable for getting the plinth, cabinet, and head shapes right.
